Description: explicit — GeoJSON vs tiles decision for a real scenario
prompt: I have about 8,000 hiking trail segments stored as GeoJSON, and users need to click a trail to see its name and distance. I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?

**Short answer:** You can start with a plain **GeoJSON source** for the 8 000 trail segments – it is well inside the “sweet-spot” for GeoJSON ( < 2 MB / < 5 000 features  is the rule-of-thumb, and 8 000 short line strings are usually still under 2 MB if you keep the geometry simple). Keep the basemap as a **vector-tile source** (most public basemaps are delivered that way) and add your trail layer on top of it. If you later find the trail file growing (more geometry detail, higher-resolution elevation data, or you want to support many concurrent mobile users) you can switch the trails to a **vector-tile source** generated with *tippecanoe* (or *Planetiler*). The switch is painless because the style will still reference a source named “trails”; you only change the source definition. Below is a concrete plan, plus the code you’ll need to wire it together. --- ## 1. Check the size of your GeoJSON | #features | Typical size (simple LineString) | |-----------|-----------------------------------| | 8 000 | ≈ 0.5 – 1.2 MB (depends on coordinate precision) | If you keep the coordinates to 5-6 decimal places (≈ 10 cm accuracy) you’ll stay comfortably under 1 MB. That is well inside the **“sweet spot”** where browsers load, parse and render instantly, even on modest phones. > **If you ever exceed ~5 MB** (e.g. you start adding elevation arrays, very detailed geometry, or you need to support many simultaneous users on low-end devices) move to vector tiles. The thresholds are in the skill table, but 8 000 short line strings are usually fine. --- ## 2. Choose the basemap source Use any public vector-tile basemap that includes terrain and road layers. Some popular free options: | Provider | URL (TileJSON) | Terrain? | Attribution | |----------|----------------|----------|-------------| | OpenMapTiles | `https://free.tilehosting.com/data/v3.json?key=YOUR_KEY` | Yes (DEM layer) | © OpenMapTiles | | MapTiler (free tier) | `https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY` | Yes (hillshade) | © MapTiler | | OpenFreeMap | `https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/standard.json` | Yes (DEM) | © OpenStreetMap contributors | All of these expose a **vector source** (or a whole style URL) that already contains separate layers for terrain, roads, water, labels, etc. You’ll just add your own source on top. --- ## 3. Wire the two sources together in a style ### 3.1. Minimal style skeleton (JSON) ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sprite": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/sprite/sprite", "sources": { "basemap": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://free.tilehosting.com/data/v3.json?key=YOUR_KEY" }, "trails": { "type": "geojson", "data": "/data/trails.geojson" } }, "layers": [ /* 1️⃣ Basemap background & terrain – keep the order the basemap style gives you */ ... (you can copy the whole `layers` array from the basemap style, or just reference the style URL directly) /* 2️⃣ Insert your trail layer *before* the first symbol layer so labels stay on top */ { "id": "trails-line", "type": "line", "source": "trails", "layout": { "line-join": "round", "line-cap": "round" }, "paint": { "line-color": "#ff7f00", "line-width": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 2, 14, 4, 18, 8 ] } }, { "id": "trails-label", "type": "symbol", "source": "trails", "source-layer": null, // not needed for GeoJSON "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-size": 12, "text-offset": [0, 1.2], "text-anchor": "top" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#000", "text-halo-color": "#fff", "text-halo-width": 1 } }, /* 3️⃣ Keep the rest of the basemap’s symbol layers (road names, place labels, etc.) */ ... (the remaining layers from the basemap style) ] } ``` **Key points** * **Insert your trail layers *before* the first symbol layer** of the basemap. That guarantees that road/place labels stay readable. The `maplibre-source-wiring` skill shows how to programmatically find the first symbol layer (`map.getStyle().layers.findIndex(l => l.type === 'symbol')`) and `splice` your layers there. * **GeoJSON source does not need a `source-layer`** – that property is only for vector tiles. * **Interaction** – you can now query the trail features directly: ```js map.on('click', 'trails-line', (e) => { const props = e.features[0].properties; new maplibregl.Popup() .setLngLat(e.lngLat) .setHTML(`${props.name}
Length: ${props.distance} km`) .addTo(map); }); ``` --- ## 4. When (and how) to migrate to vector tiles If you ever hit any of these conditions, switch the `trails` source to a vector tile set: | Condition | Migration step | |-----------|----------------| | File size > 5 MB **or** feature count > 50 k | Run **tippecanoe** (or **Planetiler**) to create a `.mbtiles` file, then serve it via a TileJSON endpoint (e.g. PMTiles, TileServer-GL, or a static S3 bucket with a simple TileJSON). | | You need different styling at different zoom levels (e.g. hide minor trails at low zoom) | Encode zoom-dependent `minzoom`/`maxzoom` in tippecanoe (`--minimum-zoom`, `--maximum-zoom`) and style those layers separately. | | You want to support offline or very low-bandwidth clients | Vector tiles are ~10-20 × smaller than the equivalent GeoJSON, and they load only the tiles that intersect the viewport. | **Tippecanoe one-liner (Linux/macOS):** ```bash tippecanoe \ --output=trails.mbtiles \ --layer=trails \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --minimum-zoom=6 \ --simplify-only-low-zoom \ --force \ trails.geojson ``` Then expose it with a tiny TileJSON file: ```json { "tiles": ["https://my.cdn.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"], "minzoom": 6, "maxzoom": 14, "attribution": "© Your Organization" } ``` In the style, replace the `trails` source definition with: ```json "trails": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://my.cdn.com/trails.tilejson" } ``` All you have to change in your style is the `type` and `url`; the layer IDs (`trails-line`, `trails-label`) stay the same, so the rest of your code (pop-ups, event listeners) works unchanged. --- ## 5. Summary checklist | ✅ | Item | |---|------| | **GeoJSON size** – confirm the file is < 2 MB (run `ls -lh trails.geojson`). | | **Basemap source** – pick a public vector-tile style URL (OpenMapTiles, MapTiler, etc.). | | **Style JSON** – add two sources (`basemap` = vector, `trails` = geojson). | | **Layer order** – insert your trail line & label layers *before* the first symbol layer of the basemap. | | **Interaction** – attach a `click` handler to `trails-line` to show name & distance. | | **Future-proofing** – keep tippecanoe/Planetiler in your toolbox; if the trail dataset grows or you need zoom-dependent styling, swap the source definition to `type: "vector"` and point at the TileJSON you generate. | That’s it! With this setup you get: * **Fast load** for the 8 000 trails (single GeoJSON fetch). * **Crisp, scalable basemap** (vector tiles) with terrain and road labels. * **Full interactivity** (click → popup) because the data stays client-side. * **A low-effort migration path** to vector tiles if the dataset ever outgrows the GeoJSON sweet spot. Happy mapping! 🚶‍♀️🗺️

Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR  
Your 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is well past the **“crash zone”** for a `geojson` source (see the table in the skill). The only practical way to get this data into a MapLibre map without killing the browser is to **serve it as vector tiles** (or, if you really can’t tile, fall back to a raster image of the layer). Below is a concise decision-tree, the minimal steps you need to take, and the tools you can use – no full build script required.

---

## 1. Why GeoJSON Won’t Work Any More

| Metric | GeoJSON limit (rule-of-thumb) | Your data |
|--------|------------------------------|-----------|
| File size | **< 2 MB** (sweet spot) → instant | **180 MB** |
| Feature count | **< 5 k** (sweet spot) → smooth | **≈ 400 k** |
| Parse time | 1–3 s for 5–20 MB | **> 10 s** (often > 30 s) |
| Memory pressure | < 50 MB | **> 300 MB** (browser-crash zone) |

MapLibre must download **the whole file**, parse it into a JavaScript object, and then build WebGL buffers. At 180 MB the parser stalls, the main thread is blocked, and the tab either freezes or is killed by the browser’s out-of-memory guard.

> **Bottom line:** Switch to a tiled source.

---

## 2. Choose the Right Tiled Source

| Use-case | Recommended source type | Why |
|----------|------------------------|-----|
| **Large vector data** (your polygons) | `vector` (MVT/MLT) | Small binary tiles, zoom-dependent detail, client-side styling & querying |
| **If you cannot generate vector tiles** | `raster` (pre-rendered PNG/JPEG) | No client-side interaction, but works for static overlays |
| **Offline / single-file deployment** | `pmtiles` (vector tiles in a single archive) | Same `vector` benefits, bundled in one file; works with the `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill |

> **Do NOT** try to keep the data as a single GeoJSON and hope compression (gzip/brotli) will save you – the parsing cost is the killer, not the download size.

---

## 3. Minimal Workflow to Get Vector Tiles

1. **Simplify & Reduce Precision**  
   *Goal:* shrink the geometry before tiling.  
   - **Tool:** `mapshaper` (CLI or web UI) – `-simplify dp 10%` and `-precision 5` (or lower)  
   - **Result:** often a 70-90 % reduction in size with negligible visual impact at typical map scales.

2. **Generate MVT (Mapbox Vector Tile) or MLT (MapLibre Tile) files**  
   - **Tippecanoe** (fast, works directly on GeoJSON):  
     ```bash
     tippecanoe \
       --output=data.mbtiles \
       --layer=parcels \
       --drop-densest-as-needed \
       --maximum-zoom=14 \
       --minimum-zoom=5 \
       --simplify-only-low-zooms \
       --force \
       simplified.geojson
     ```
   - **Planetiler** (Java-based, good for huge OSM-style pipelines) if you need custom attribute handling or want to generate MLT directly.  
   - Both produce an **MBTiles** SQLite container.

3. **Serve the tiles**  
   - **Option A – Tile server** (e.g. `tileserver-gl`, `tileserver-php`, or any static-file server that can read MBTiles).  
   - **Option B – Server-less PMTiles**:  
     ```bash
     # Convert MBTiles → PMTiles
     mbutil data.mbtiles ./tiles/   # extracts .pbf tiles
     pmtiles create data.pmtiles ./tiles/
     ```
     Then host `data.pmtiles` on a CDN or static bucket and use the `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill to add it as a source.

4. **Add the source to your MapLibre style**  
   ```javascript
   map.addSource('parcels', {
     type: 'vector',
     url: 'https://my.cdn.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'   // or a TileJSON URL if you use a tile server
   });

   map.addLayer({
     id: 'parcel-fill',
     type: 'fill',
     source: 'parcels',
     'source-layer': 'parcels',   // name you gave in tippecanoe (--layer)
     paint: {
       'fill-color': '#ff6600',
       'fill-opacity': 0.4
     }
   });
   ```

5. **(Optional) Keep a tiny GeoJSON for the lowest zoom**  
   If you want a quick “overview” before any tiles load, create a **very-simplified** version (e.g. < 2 MB, < 5 k polygons) and add it as a separate `geojson` source that you show only at `maxzoom: 5`. Then hide it once the vector tiles appear.

---

## 4. What If You Must Stay in the Browser (No Tile Server)?

*Use **PMTiles** – a single file that the browser can fetch via HTTP range requests.*  
- Host `data.pmtiles` on any static file host (GitHub Pages, S3, Cloudflare R2).  
- In MapLibre, add the source with the `pmtiles` protocol (the `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill sets up the custom protocol handler).  
- This gives you the same performance as a normal vector source but without a separate tile-server process.

---

## 5. Quick “What-If” Checklist

| Question | Answer → Action |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Do I need per-feature interactivity (click/hover)?** | Yes → stay with vector tiles (MVT/MLT). |
| **Do I need the layer to be printable as a raster image?** | No → vector tiles are fine; you can rasterize on the client if needed. |
| **Can I afford a small server or a CDN?** | Yes → host MBTiles via `tileserver-gl` or static `.pbf` tiles. |
| **Is the app completely offline?** | Use a single `pmtiles` archive. |
| **Do I only need a static image of the parcels?** | Render the layer once (e.g., with QGIS or GDAL) to a raster tile set and use a `raster` source. |
| **Do I need to support older browsers that can’t do range requests?** | Serve regular `.pbf` tiles via a tile server (they work everywhere). |

---

## 6. Gotchas & Tips

| Issue | Fix / Tip |
|-------|-----------|
| **CORS errors** when fetching tiles from another domain | Ensure the tile server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| **Labels from the basemap get hidden by your fill layer** | Insert your layer **before** the first symbol layer in the style (or use `map.moveLayer('parcel-fill', 'road-label')`). |
| **Tile size blows up** after tiling | Use `--drop-densest-as-needed` (Tippecanoe) or `--max-zoom` to limit detail at high zooms. |
| **Feature properties missing** | Tippecanoe drops attributes by default; add `--preserve-input-order` or `--no-feature-limit` and list needed fields with `--attribute-filter`. |
| **Browser still stalls on initial load** | Verify you are not loading the whole MBTiles file; only the needed tiles should be requested (check network tab). |
| **Need 3-D terrain underneath** | Add a `raster-dem` source (e.g., MapTiler DEM) and enable `map.setTerrain({source: 'dem', exaggeration: 1.5})`. |

---

## 7. Next-Step Resources

| Topic | Link |
|-------|------|
| **Tippecanoe docs** | <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| **Planetiler docs** | <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |
| **PMTiles format & JS loader** | <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles> |
| **MapLibre source wiring (how to reference vector tiles)** | <../maplibre-source-wiring/SKILL.md> |
| **MapLibre-GL-Leaflet (if you still need a Leaflet wrapper)** | <https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-gl-leaflet> |
| **Raster-DEM terrain example** | <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/examples/terrain/> |

---

### Bottom Line

Your 180 MB GeoJSON is far beyond what a `geojson` source can handle in a browser. Convert the data to **vector tiles** (MVT or MLT) using **Tippecanoe** (or **Planetiler** for larger pipelines), optionally bundle them as a **PMTiles** archive for server-less delivery, and add them to the map as a `vector` source. This will shrink the network payload to a few kilobytes per tile, keep memory usage low, and restore interactivity.

If you cannot generate tiles at all, the only fallback is a **raster** image of the layer, but you’ll lose click/hover queries and styling flexibility.

Give the simplified-then-tiled workflow a try—your map will load in seconds instead of minutes, and the browser will stay alive. Happy tiling!
